pageCache.text:
Let your light shine
Welcome to our new Website!
Schools, nowadays, are so rigorously inspected, monitored, analysed and scrutinised that it is far too easy to focus on league tables and data and forget about the happiness and general well-being of the children we entrust to them. In order to learn, children need to attend school regularly and happily so it’s really important that we don’t undervalue all the stuff that goes on around the, so-called, core subjects. Don’t get me wrong! Teachers work and plan tirelessly in order to make the learning of English grammar or improper fractions relevant and fun but I’m guessing it’s probably not this that motivated your child to get out of bed this morning.
More likely; it is the exciting topic that ties all their learning together, a trip to the woods for Forest School, music, art, drama, PE, , looking after the chickens at lunch time or the excited anticipation of their favourite club at the end of the day. It is also really important that children get to share and celebrate their out-of-school news and achievements. Without showing an interest and doing a little probing it is easy to be ignorant to the fact that one of your children captains their local rugby team, is wonderful with animals, is a carer within their own family, is a gifted ballet dancer, a budding actor, a brilliant magician or has just passed entrance exams and been accepted into a prestigious public school;
The pressures wrought on teachers and children by the expectations of the National Curriculum, in its current guise, make it more important than ever that schools are thoughtful and skilful in the way in which they weave back in the fun, creativity and pure joy of learning through play and discovery.
An outstanding school is the one that your child skips happily to in the morning and leaves tired (and maybe, even a little bit grumpy) at the end of the day.
Debbie Burnett, Headteacher

SEND
Fittleworth Church of England Village School CE School
SEND Information Report March 2026.
As an inclusive school we support all children. We provide access to a broad and curriculum for all pupils, who, at any time, might need additional support with regard to their academic, emotional, social, or physical and mental health needs. Equity of opportunity is an essential reality for all of our children. We provide child centred, supportive, nurturing learning environments, enabling all pupils to maximise progress. Across our school, all staff work in accordance with the guidance provided in the Special Educational Needs & Disability (SEND) Code of Practice 2014 and Keeping Children Safe in Education September 2025.
SEND contact details
If your child has been identified as having additional needs, has a disability, or you would like to know more about what we can offer, then please feel free to contact us. Our named Inclusion Manager (Inclusion Manager - Special Educational Needs & Disability Co-ordinator) is Mrs Louise Hayter (lhayter@fittleworth.school).
Fittleworth Church of England Village School: 01798 865419
Mrs Debbie Burnett (head teacher), Mrs Sarah Blackwood (Senior Teacher) & Mr James Russell (Senior Teacher), are also available to offer advice/support and to hear your views. Class teachers are highly trained in adaptive learning experiences and as your child’s class teacher, we would highly recommend you approach them with any concerns you may have. They too, can be contacted on the above telephone numbers.
West Sussex Local Authority also maintain a SEND directory known as the Local Offer. This can be accessed at: https://westsussex.local-offer.org/
What kinds of Special Educational Needs and Disabilities are provided for at this school?
Fittleworth Church of England Village School is an inclusive, mainstream primary school. Our aim is to ensure that every one of our children thrive and meet their full potential, adaptions are made for all, regardless of need. The emotional, social, and mental wellbeing of all members of our school community is at the heart of all we do; the wellbeing of every child and their family matter to us.
Currently, we support children in all four areas of special educational need (cognition and learning, social, emotional, and mental health, communication and interaction and physical/sensory need). We support families in need, looked after children and young carers, , children who have English as a second language and those at risk of exclusion.
How do we identify a child who may have a special educational need or disability?
Children may have an identified need on entry to school, or may develop a need requiring special educational provision at any time throughout their school career. All teachers at our school are responsible for developing a secure knowledge of each child in their class, through discussion with parents and by monitoring progress through gentle, regular assessment.
Across our school, we maintain a dynamic SEND register to ensure children are receiving the adaptions and support they require to access every part of our school day. Our SEND register has clear entry and exit data. As parents, you will be consulted if we feel it is appropriate to add your child to the SEND register. We use the basis of the SEND Code of Practice to add a child to our SEND register, namely section 6.15: A pupil has SEN where their learning difficulty or disability calls for special educational provision, namely provision different from or additional to that normally available to pupils of the same age.
All children at our school receive the same high‑quality universal provision as a foundation. We discuss all children in our school in termly ‘Pupil Progress Meetings’ that involve collaborative conversation and sharing of assessment between the class teacher, SENCO and head teacher. If we have concerns about a child’s development or progress—such as if they are not working in line with their peers or their progress is slow—the class teacher will monitor a child through the Graduated Approach.
Within this approach, we identify the specific concerns and outline the additional adaptations that will be put in place and trialled. Each child is given individual outcomes (goals) so that their progress can be closely monitored. This is always done in consultation with parents. We value both child and parent/carer voice as an important part of the process.
The Graduated Approach involved a cycle of four elements.
We assess where we believe a child is at. We plan how to best support them. We ensure the support is carried out (we ‘do’ it) and then we review how this impacted a child’s progress.
For children who do not make progress against these initial APDR cycles the school, alongside parents, will make the decision to add a child to our Inclusion Register as ‘SEN Support’ We will also decide whether external referrals to clinicians or more specialist practitioners and teams are appropriate. If progress remains slow or, the gap between their functioning and that of their peers remains, then further clinical information about the child’s needs are needed to inform approaches, responses, and interventions. This data is recorded on our school system “Brom Com” and is called by the Local Authority each term. Once the child reaches this stage of our register, they will receive an Individual Learning Plan (ILP), which is based upon the APDR cycle. This document outlines the very specific outcomes set for this child and the expected progress points. Often these plans include advice from outside agencies. These plans are shared with parents.
How do we provide for children with SEND?
- monitoring of provision
- reviewing progress
a) How is the provision monitored for its effectiveness?
Children who have been highlighted as requiring extra support or intervention are monitored against personalised outcomes linked to the adaptions or intervention they are receiving via their ILP. Clear baselines are determined for all outcomes set so that we can easily track progress made. Termly learning walks occur so that leaders can be sure adaptions and interventions are being run and maintained. ‘Book Looks’ are also completed to ensure adapted learning is available for learners.
b) What are the school’s arrangements for assessing and reviewing progress of children with SEND?
We follow the Code of Practice’s cycle of ‘Assess, Plan, Do, Review’. Teachers and the Inclusion Manager regularly assess the progress of children receiving support against their personal outcomes. Opportunities to regularly revisit new learning from interventions within whole class teaching helps to embed new skills learnt.
Reviewing outcomes can be fluid, depending on progress made. Class teachers review outcomes on a half termly basis so that support can be put in place in an appropriate and timely manner. ILPS are reviewed and re-written termly and shared with parents. Parents are encouraged to be a part of this process and add their views to the documents shared with them.
c) What is the school’s approach to teaching children with SEND?
Across our School, all children receive high quality class-based teaching, this is reviewed regularly and robustly throughout each term. As part of this Quality First teaching, the class teacher will provide adapted work based on the needs of the child. If it is felt that a child is not making expected progress then a graduated response will be adopted using the Assess, Plan, Do, Review approach. We offer a wide variety of evidence-based interventions as well as adult supported group work which is carefully monitored to ensure that there is an impact on children’s learning. All support is recorded on an individual learning (ILP). The format used, depends on the level of support an individual is receiving. ILPs outline the expected outcome of the support; these are formally reviewed termly but are seen as a fluid document. We also deliver therapy specified by outside agencies and endeavour to incorporate these targets into everyday teaching. Changes may be made to provision before the review date set.
d) How does the school adapt the curriculum and learning environment for children with SEND?
The type of support needed for each child to make good progress will depend on the needs of the child.
Adaptions are considered at every level and extend further than solely academic progress. For children with additional need, we will consider adaptions against every school-based experience. At our school, we tailor learning so that every child can take part, succeed and feel confident. Teachers make thoughtful, needs‑led adaptations within lessons—such as breaking tasks into smaller steps, providing visual prompts, offering alternative ways to record work, or giving additional adult support when needed. We use flexible groupings, carefully chosen resources and a calm, structured classroom environment to reduce barriers and help children stay focused. These adaptations are part of everyday teaching, ensuring pupils with SEND learn alongside their peers while receiving the personalised support that helps them thrive.
We use the Education Endowment Foundation Five a Day principle as a basis for our adaptive practice. EEF blog: The Five-a-day approach: How the EEF can support | EEF
e) What additional support is available for children with SEND?
We offer a range of support to ensure children with SEND can access learning and make good progress. This includes high‑quality, differentiated teaching in every classroom, targeted small‑group interventions, and individual support tailored to specific needs. Our staff work closely with external professionals—such as speech and language therapists, educational psychologists and health specialists—to provide additional guidance where needed. We also use personalised strategies, supportive resources, and regular check‑ins to help children feel secure and confident in school. All support is reviewed regularly with parents to ensure it continues to meet each child’s needs effectively.
f) How does the school enable pupils with SEND to engage in the activities of the school (including physical activities) together with children who do not have special needs?
Clubs, trips, and activities offered to our pupils are fully accessible to all. Where necessary, we will seek advice to support children in particular lessons such as PE and we also ensure that outside providers follow the advice given. Where an activity may not be suitable for children we will make ‘best endeavours’ to adapt it so that all pupils receive a similar outcome.
Children work alongside each other and children with SEND are not segregated from children without SEND.
g) What support is available for ensuring the emotional and social development of pupils with SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities)?
We care deeply about the social, emotional, and mental health needs of all the children at Fittleworth Church of England Village School. As a small school, we build strong relationships with all our children and families. The Inclusion Manager takes additional responsibility for building a relationship with each child & family on the SEND register for the children to feel free to share emotional and social concerns and to build strategies together to solve problems. Pastoral support can also be provided by the child’s class teacher, as well as accessing a Local Authority Family Support Worker where appropriate. We have a trained ELSA (Emotional Literacy Support Assistant) who is available to work with children referred through Pupil Progress Meetings.
We are a fully inclusive school with a detailed positive behaviour policy that enables children to be aware of our high expectations. We work closely with those children who struggle to manage their behaviour, to ensure that they have opportunities to express themselves appropriately. We adopt a no shame or judgement policy when supporting our children and work hard to develop the acceptance of others around different needs.
For children who require more specialised support, where funding allows, we can access play therapists and community liaison services.
Who is the named SEND contact?
Our SEND named contact is Mrs Louise Hayter
What specific expertise is available for those with SEND?
Staff receive regular professional development which will include a focus on inclusion and SEND support. For example, all staff undertake auto injector pen training annually, and the school nurse will deliver training on other health issues. Staff have completed training on a range of mental health, social and behaviour issues. Most recent SEND training for staff from outside agencies (2025-2026) has been in supporting dyslexia, working memory, autism, behaviour and precision teaching techniques. There is ongoing training in adaptive teaching via staff meetings.
What specialist equipment and facilities are there for children with SEND?
An accessible parking space is available. There is a ramp facility to allow easy access into the main school building.
We have a large field and garden area.
We have a small medical room, which can be used for personal care, with it’s own toilet.
We work with a variety of outside agencies to provide specialist equipment and facilities for children with SEND to ensure that they can fully access the curriculum.
For more information, please see the school’s Accessibility Plan.
Admission of disabled students
Access to all classrooms is possible via our playground entrances. Our site is on one level and maintains good access to all areas.
Accessibility is supported through our accessibility plan (see school website) and under our duty of care stated in the Disability and Equality Act 2010.
What steps do we take to prevent pupils with SEND being treated less favorably than other pupils?

Breakfast Club
We run a daily breakfast club for the benefit of children attending our school. It runs Monday to Thursday from 7.45am-8.45am.
It is staffed by our learning support assistants who offer breakfast plus a wide range of activities.
You do not have to book in advance, just use MCAS to pay/book for a place.
£3 per session for pupil premium children.
Our club is registered with Chichester District Council and we have a 5* food rating!
Our breakfast menu includes a variety of cereals, toast and various toppings.
If you have any questions please contact Liz Wilmshurst on the school office. 01798 865419 or lwilmshurst@fittleworth.school
Breakfast Club

Attendance/Absence
Your child's attendance at school is very important to us.
Every child is entitled by law to good, full time education that meets their needs. It is your responsibility as parents to ensure that your child attends school every day that we are open except in a small number of allowable circumstances such as your child being too ill to attend or being given permission for an absence in advance from the school. (In exceptional circumstances only)
We monitor attendance very carefully and will do everything we can to help you enable your child to attend school. We ask that you do not take your children out of school for holidays, birthday treats, family get togethers or any other reason unless it is truly exceptional.
Every day that your child misses school is a day of education lost that your child is entitled to.
If you do intend to take your child out of school you must first apply to us for consent using the form that can be found below. A paper copy is also available in the office.
If you have any questions relating to any attendance matters please do not hesitate to contact either Mrs Burnett or Mrs Wilmshurst.
If your child is too poorly to come to school, please call or email office@fittleworth.school by 9.30am to give reasons for absence.

Our Curriculum
Fittleworth CE School provides a creative curriculum to promote the intellectual, physical, social, emotional and spiritual development of the individual child.
The school is committed to first hand experience and learning. This experience is gained through events and practical experiences at school incl. visitors and visits to places of interest in the locality and the study of real artefacts and documents. The children’s work is displayed and celebrated throughout the school. We encourage children to share and celebrate their work with their families and carers. Children are taught individually, in groups or as a whole class as appropriate to the context of the teaching and their individual needs
We are a local authority maintained school and as such are required to deliver the national curriculum to all of our pupils. The national curriculum sets out the programmes of study and attainment targets for all subjects at all 4 key stages and at primary level is made up of the following subjects:
Literacy

pageCache.pageTitle: Fittleworth CofE Village School - Forest School
pageCache.text:
Forest School
The aim of forest schooling is to develop the skills of collaboration, cooperation, team building and awareness of the natural environment. The children in years 1-6 will spend a minimum of six sessions in the woods. They will develop their knowledge and understanding of the natural world and their forest school woodland in particular. It will become their special place and a sense of stewardship is crucial to the ethos of out forest school. Children will make their own choices, whilst understanding the risks and challenges of the task that they complete. Children will improve their understanding and appreciation of their outside environment and the impact of their own actions on a place. The children will be in the forest led by Mrs. Bugle, supported by other members of staff and parent helpers as our aim is to provide a very high adult/child ratio.
We use a piece of private woodland adjacent to Limbourne Lane, Fittleworth and we access Fittleworth Common. We are also currently planning an onsite Forest School area within our grounds so watch this space!
The children will take part in a range of tasks including:
Exploring
Helping to light our fire
Gather wood for our fire
Learn to recognise animal tracks
Shelter building
Learn to use tools safely.
